key_insight: SEMA3G levels were lower in Alzheimer’s disease and frontotemporal dementia, but plasma levels did not distinguish cerebral amyloid angiopathy–associated MRI burden.
clinical_relevance: These findings do not support plasma SEMA3G for identifying higher cerebral amyloid angiopathy burden in memory clinic patients.
method: Compared SEMA3G across diagnoses in GNPC cerebrospinal fluid (n=1,982) and plasma (n=6,917) datasets.
Assessed longitudinal plasma SEMA3G changes in mild cognitive impairment and Alzheimer’s disease.
Evaluated plasma SEMA3G against MRI lobar microbleed groups (0, 1–2, ≥3) in 161 memory clinic participants.
evidence_signal: Plasma SEMA3G declined over time in mild cognitive impairment and Alzheimer’s disease, but was not associated with microbleed burden, white matter hyperintensities, or plasma amyloid-beta isoforms in the memory clinic cohort.
watch_item: Microbleeds were a proxy for cerebral amyloid angiopathy; validation in genetically susceptible or neuropathologically confirmed cohorts remains needed.
paper_title: Evaluation of Semaphorin 3G (SEMA3G) as a biofluid biomarker of cerebral amyloid angiopathy: evidence from neurodegenerative disease and memory clinic cohorts
